papers.title: Can Image Generators Hold a Scene Together When Space Is Broken Apart?
papers.abstract_en: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.

papers.title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
papers.abstract_en: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.

papers.title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models
papers.abstract_en: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.

papers.title: Integrated GPU Core for Mamba-3
papers.abstract_en: Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. However, its multi-input multi-output (MIMO) computation, exponential-trapezoidal discretization, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) introduce dense, element-wise, and sequential operations. Despite kernel fusion, conventional GPUs execute these operations inefficiently. Our characterization of Mamba-3 hybrid models reveals numerous kernel launches, substantial data movement, and increased register pressure that reduces warp occupancy and memory-latency hiding. We propose RescuCore, a specialized GPU execution unit for Mamba-3 inference that retains other hybrid model layers on existing GPU resources. Integrated alongside CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) sub-partition, RescuCore shares the register file, shared memory, and warp schedulers. Dense projections remain on conventional GPU resources, while RescuCore pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO computation, recurrent state updates, and output gating to reduce kernel fragmentation and intermediate data movement. We select BF16 after evaluating multiple numerical formats, preserving model accuracy with an estimated area overhead of 5.9% of an A100 die for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4. We evaluate RescuCore using cycle-accurate Accel-Sim simulation, RTL synthesis, and synthesis-informed AccelWattch power modeling. Compared with conventional GPU execution, RescuCore achieves 1.4-9.4x speedup and 1.4-5.0x energy reduction during prefill, and 1.3-2.8x speedup and 1.2-2.6x energy reduction during autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the potential of GPU-integrated specialized execution for SSM-based hybrid models.

papers.title: QA-CMIF:Accurate and Lightweight Cross-Modal Latent Imputation and Fusion for Fault-Tolerant sEMG-Inertial Hand Gesture Recognition
papers.abstract_en: Fusing surface electromyography (sEMG) with inertial measurements is widely used for myoelectric prosthesis control and wearable human-machine interfaces. In daily wear, however, socket micro-displacement, electrode lift-off, and wire failures often corrupt an unknown subset of sEMG channels through burst artifacts, lift-off shocks, or open-circuit dropouts. Existing fusion networks mix all channels in the first convolutional layer, so a few corrupted electrodes contaminate the entire latent representation, whereas gate-only attenuation of corrupted channels discards the co-activation cues needed to separate fine-grained gestures. We propose QA-CMIF, a quality-aware cross-modal latent imputation and fusion framework that encodes each sEMG channel independently, scores its reliability with a soft gate, and protects intact channels via a confidence-weighted residual bypass, while a cross-attention imputer repairs degraded channels in latent space using the inertial stream and remaining reliable sEMG channels under a bad-channel alignment loss. Across within-subject evaluations on 29 participants from Ninapro DB3, DB2, and DB5 spanning 17-52 gesture classes, QA-CMIF outperformed the gate-only baseline under 50% channel corruption by 1.29-2.65 percentage points, denoted pp, across all three 17-class cohorts with paired-t Holm-adjusted p<0.002, widened this margin to 2.59-4.15 pp on the 40- and 52-class tasks, and surpassed corruption-augmented conventional fusion by 4.61-19.85 pp. Requiring only 0.175-0.185M parameters and 2.45-2.63M multiply-accumulate operations across the 2000 Hz and 200 Hz setups, QA-CMIF saves 46%-55% in parameters and 72%-81% in compute over recent baselines with a 1.44 ms 99th-percentile single-thread CPU latency.

papers.title: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction
papers.abstract_en: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The project page is available at https://sgip2026.github.io.

papers.title: HIVE-ECIA: Identity-Aware Historical Evidence Acquisition for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Object Tracking
papers.abstract_en: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360° field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.

papers.title: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization
papers.abstract_en: We consider regularized nonconvex optimization over a closed convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, which involves a convex nonsmooth regularizer $r$ in the objective and $n$ smooth equality constraints. To find a near-KKT point of the problem, we propose a prox-linear first-order method, named as SEPi-Prox, based on a smoothed exact-penalty formulation. At each outer iteration of SEPi-Prox, a strongly convex prox-linear subproblem is formed and solved inexactly to a sufficient accuracy. Under a local non-singularity condition that is weaker than some other commonly used regularity conditions or constraint qualifications, SEPi-Prox finds an $ε$-KKT point within $O(ε^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls, matching the lower bound for unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We employ Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient method (APG) and a dual cutting-plane method (DCP) for the prox-linear subproblems. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_r$ denote the numbers of arithmetic operations of evaluating one first-order oracle and one proximal mapping of $r$ over $\mathcal{X}$, respectively. Then SEPi-Prox requires $\widetilde{O}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}ε^{-2} + (dn + \mathcal{C}_r)ε^{-5/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}((\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}} + dn^2 + n\mathcal{C}_r + n^{3.373})ε^{-2})$ total arithmetic operations to produce an $ε$-KKT point, respectively by using APG and DCP as the subsolver. The latter result is preferable when $n$ is small and nearly matches the optimal dependence on $ε$. Numerical experiments on instances of the multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification demonstrate the efficiency of SEPi-Prox with both subsolvers.

papers.title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
papers.abstract_en: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

papers.title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
papers.abstract_en: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

papers.title: Relax-and-Sparsify Approximation Algorithms for Sparse Ridge Regression
papers.abstract_en: This paper studies sparse ridge regression in the low-rank, high-dimensional setting that often arises when data collection is expensive. By exploiting the low-rank structure, we develop approximation algorithms within a relax-and-sparsify framework: solve a convex relaxation and then sparsify its solution to satisfy the original sparsity constraint. Specifically, we establish a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound for the convex relaxation by decomposing its support into two parts. This decomposition in turn motivates two approximation strategies, parameter reduction and binary redistribution, each exploiting a different part. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the binary redistribution algorithms outperform the benchmarks in most instances.

papers.title: An Interpretable Acoustic Coordinate System for Japanese Consonant Morae in Dysarthric Speech
papers.abstract_en: Dysarthria reduces speech intelligibility, requiring self-directed rehabilitation based on fine-grained feedback to capture gradual articulatory changes. For Japanese speakers, such feedback is naturally provided in mora units due to its distinct moraic timing and consonant-vowel structure. While recent visualization methods have explored distance-based feedback, most are limited to vowels. Extending them to consonants is challenging, as generative embeddings often smooth transient spectral structures. We propose a visualization system for Japanese consonant morae that maps articulatory deviations onto a two-dimensional space defined by temporal and spectral distances from healthy reference speech. Experiments show consistent geometric separation of consonant categories, with Silhouette Coefficients exceeding 0.5 and origin-based ROC-AUC scores above 0.86. Furthermore, evaluations using real dysarthric speech achieved a high ROC-AUC of 0.897 in screening for unclear pronunciations. Perturbation tests confirm orthogonal temporal and spectral shifts, yielding a physically interpretable mapping for rehabilitation.

papers.title: Floorplan-Context-Aware Cross-Environment Human Activity Recognition from mmWave Radar Point Clouds
papers.abstract_en: Human activity recognition (HAR) models based on mmWave radar point clouds and trained in controlled open spaces often experience performance degradation when deployed in furnished rooms. We propose a Floorplan-Context-Aware (FCA) HAR enhancement method that augments the input with subject-furniture relative position information to improve cross-environment performance. Because existing mmWave point-cloud datasets lack registered floorplans, we introduce a pseudo-landmark augmentation strategy for training the FCA model. In cross-environment evaluation on the mm-ADL-Home dataset, FCA achieves 77.70% accuracy and 65.49% macro-F1, improving upon the point-cloud-only direct-transfer baseline by 10.73 and 10.05 percentage points, respectively, and exceeding the strongest evaluated adaptation baseline by 7.37 and 6.27 percentage points. At deployment, FCA requires only a one-time registration of furniture landmarks, with no target-domain activity annotations or model weight updates.

papers.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
papers.abstract_en: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

papers.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark
papers.abstract_en: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.

papers.title: StyleJudge: A Human-Validated, In-Context-Learning Vision-Language Evaluator for Artistic Style Transfer
papers.abstract_en: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.

papers.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

papers.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

papers.title: FinVerify: A Verification Framework for Financial Agents
papers.abstract_en: Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.

papers.title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
papers.abstract_en: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

papers.title: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
papers.abstract_en: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.abstract_en: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

papers.title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
papers.abstract_en: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

papers.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
papers.abstract_en: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

papers.title: It Depends on the Task: Rethinking Rhetorical Segmentation of Dutch Judicial Decisions
papers.abstract_en: Classifying the material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision (rhetorical roles) in case law is a prerequisite for high-quality performance across virtually all NLP-in-law tasks, including legal information retrieval, summarisation, and LLM-based analysis. These rhetorical roles often intertwine and shift sentence by sentence, making reliable classification difficult. This paper introduces the first sentence-level annotated dataset of Dutch judicial decisions, labelled across four legally meaningful categories: material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision, alongside non-annotated (None) content, and compares several classification strategies, including a staged pipeline that separates None detection from the rhetorical roles, and a Bayesian update that leverages information about the section-header a sentence belongs to. Our results show that no single strategy dominates on both precision and recall: header priors help most when the None sentences are excluded and offer little benefit for None detection itself. These trade-offs matter in practice. For instance, extractive summarisation depends more on recall so it does not miss relevant facts, whereas outcome prediction depends more on precision regarding decision and facts sentences so that the predicted ruling is not contaminated by noise. We use these trade-offs and map the approaches tested in this study onto a set of representative legal NLP use cases.

papers.title: CapCover Filter: Semantic Approximate Membership Queries over Embeddings
papers.abstract_en: Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives. We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput. Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.abstract_en: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

papers.title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
papers.abstract_en: Lab-in-the-loop systems, in which a model proposes molecules, automated assays measure their properties and the results retrain the model, are a popular approach to antibody lead optimization. These systems optimize for a specification defined with metrics computed from instrument signals, so their success depends on how well those metrics serve as proxies for the properties a drug candidate needs. When a metric is a poor proxy, neither a better model nor more data will fix it, and identifying the problem usually requires expert review. We report two campaigns run on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform, one on an anti-albumin nanobody (VHH) and one on an anti-mesothelin single-chain variable fragment (scFv), in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop. Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants we built libraries from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics, and found from the raw curves that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied. The libraries were built as controlled comparisons, so the results also show what each mutation contributes to each property. We fit a physical model of the curves, used it to choose metrics suited to each scaffold, and changed the experimental protocol, varying protein concentration and heating rate, to test the model against pre-registered predictions. Both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.

papers.title: Learning Spatially Aware Audio-Visual Features from Videos with Mono Audio
papers.abstract_en: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
papers.abstract_en: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

papers.title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
papers.abstract_en: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

papers.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
papers.abstract_en: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

papers.title: Practical Semantic Communication for General-Purpose Networks: Compression of High-Dimensional Embeddings Under Quantization
papers.abstract_en: This paper introduces a practical framework for semantic communication over wireless channels, focusing on the compression of high-dimensional embeddings under quantization and channel errors. Building upon a relaxed Gaussian Information Bottleneck (GIB) model, the approach provides analytical solutions for task-relevant information preservation, even with non-Gaussian targets. The framework relaxes traditional Gaussian assumptions, enabling effective compression for discrete and complex data such as text embeddings. It derives closed-form gradients for optimizing the compression matrix and establishes bounds linking continuous representations to discrete, noisy system performance. Comprehensive experiments on text classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms task-agnostic quantization-based compression methods, maintaining high semantic fidelity at low bit budgets per embedding. The approach offers a scalable, interpretable, and resource-efficient solution for deploying semantic communication in general-purpose networks.

papers.title: acuSimNet: Multi-View Self-Occlusion-Awared Visibility Learning for Cranio-Cervical Acupuncture Points
papers.abstract_en: The localization of acupuncture points (acupoints) in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) presents unique challenges since they are defined by abstract principles rather than distinct anatomical landmarks. Existing approaches are typically constrained to single view or rely on indirect calculations of relative positions with respect to other landmarks, thereby overlooking human anatomical variations. Furthermore, acupoint visibility assessment, which determins whether points are occluded by human itself, hair, clothing, or other objects, has received limited attention in practical applications. Acupoint localization itself does not require 3D reconstruction, but inferring their occlusion relationships with anatomical surfaces does, which adds computational cost and limits real-time inference. In this work, we introduce acuSimNet, an efficient hierarchical multi-task learning architecture for multi-view, self-occlusion-aware visibility prediction of acupoints, achieving 99.97% accuracy on the validation set. Our approach also addresses the challenges of high-dimensional classification (174 acupoints in cervicocranial region), negative convergence issues for visible acupoints, and inter-task scheduling optimization, resulting in substantially accelerated convergence. We improved the training efficiency from the exisiting methods of 3000 epochs to achieve 99% validation accuracy, to our optimized framework achieving 90% accuracy in 39 epochs and 99% accuracy in 86 epochs. This architecture overcomes the limitations of existing methods, could enable practical applications in acupoints detection and visualization, advancing the automation of TCM.

papers.title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
papers.abstract_en: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

papers.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
papers.abstract_en: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

papers.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
papers.abstract_en: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

papers.title: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA
papers.abstract_en: Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. A striking implication of the original work is that a model trained on only 33% ambiguous examples can outperform full-data training on several OOD evaluations, including a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD evaluated on Adversarial SQuAD. We revisit this claim in a stricter setting: open-ended extractive question answering, where models must predict answer spans rather than classify question-sentence pairs. For each encoder family, we compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics, train on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial-only AddSent and AddOneSent rows. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. These results show that clean-source cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not carry over as a general replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.

papers.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
papers.abstract_en: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

papers.title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation
papers.abstract_en: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.

papers.title: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
papers.abstract_en: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
papers.abstract_en: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

papers.title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
papers.abstract_en: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.

papers.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
papers.abstract_en: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

papers.title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents
papers.abstract_en: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

papers.title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
papers.abstract_en: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

papers.title: Equal Dose, Different Coverage:Tracing Rate and Duration in Image Editing
papers.abstract_en: Benchmarks for scientific image editing test whether a model draws the outcome of a described process, leaving open which representations carry its errors and whether correcting them yields the right quantity. We study this question with an airbrush of fixed deposition profile, under which exchanging rate and duration preserves the dose and should preserve the endpoint, yet changes the edited coverage. Matched-norm activation patches across text positions and denoising stages show that, in distilled FLUX with Chinese prompts, representations at unchanged text positions (context) carry this discrepancy: early context transfers 3.51 of the 3.98 percentage-point (pp) signed route difference, against 0.09 pp for equal-norm updates at the two changed digits. Early image latents transmit native (unpatched) route differences across two FLUX configurations and OmniGen, while text-position effects depend on configuration. The trace predicts an intervention: share early context between routes while each retains its own digits. On independent English layouts, this reduces the distilled-FLUX absolute route gap from 1.13 to 0.60 pp, outperforms early digit sharing, and improves agreement more than in base FLUX under directly paired tests. Calibrated evaluation, which prescribes an area for each dose, separates this gain from accuracy: sharing the full prompt encoding produces identical route images with target errors of 8-16 pp, and stating the target percentage directly retains a compressed area response. Localization predicts a consistency gain on new layouts, and calibration measures the quantity error that agreement leaves unresolved.

papers.title: PRISM: Primitive-Integrated Separable Modulation with Priority Visual Memory Queue for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
papers.abstract_en: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.

papers.title: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
papers.abstract_en: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

papers.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
papers.abstract_en: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.
